long: Opening post. Uniswap v2 sets the price of every swap with a single invariant, x · y = k, enforced by a smart contract: no order book, no market maker, nobody in the middle. Lending markets, stablecoins and vaults follow the same pattern: short public formulas anyone can check on-chain. The series takes those formulas one per post, with their edge cases and the incidents that exposed them.
tech: #DeFi Mechanics #1: Uniswap v2 prices every swap with one invariant, x · y = k, run by a smart contract. Lending, stablecoins and vaults work the same way: public formulas, no trader in the middle. One formula per post, starting now.
simple: #DeFi Mechanics #1: A decentralized exchange has no order book and no market maker. A short formula sets every price, and anyone can check it on-chain. This series opens those formulas one by one.

card.title: One formula prices every swap
card.sub: No order book, no market maker. This series opens those public formulas one by one.

long: Constant product AMM (Uniswap v2): the pool's two reserves x and y must keep x · y = k, fees aside. Swapping Δx in returns Δy = y · Δx / (x + Δx). The curve is a hyperbola, so neither reserve can ever be emptied: each further unit just gets more expensive. Plain version: multiply the two amounts, the product must stay the same after each trade, so taking one token out means putting more of the other in.
tech: #DeFi Mechanics #2: Constant product AMM: reserves x and y must satisfy x · y = k. A swap of Δx in returns Δy = y · Δx / (x + Δx), fees aside. The curve is a hyperbola: you can never empty either side, only make it ever more expensive.
simple: #DeFi Mechanics #2: Uniswap's rule is x · y = k. A pool holds two tokens, and after every trade the amounts multiplied together must stay the same (before fees). Take some of one token out, and you must put more of the other in.

card.title: Why a pool can never run dry
card.sub: The product of both reserves stays fixed, so each extra unit costs more than the last.

long: In an x · y = k pool, the marginal (spot) price of x in terms of y is y / x, the slope of the curve. The pool has no price feed: its price is just what the reserves say after the last swap. Example: 100 ETH and 300,000 USDC means 1 ETH ≈ 3,000 USDC. Every trade changes the reserves, so every trade moves the price.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #3: In a constant product pool, the marginal (spot) price of x in terms of y is y / x, the slope of the curve x · y = k. There is no price feed inside the pool.

The price is whatever the reserves say after the last swap. Example: 100 ETH and 300,000 USDC means 1 ETH ≈ 3,000 USDC. Every trade changes the reserves, so every trade moves the price.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #3: In a Uniswap-style pool, the price is just a ratio: 100 ETH and 300,000 USDC in the pool means 1 ETH ≈ 3,000 USDC. Every trade changes the amounts, so every trade moves the price.

Buy ETH, and there's less ETH and more USDC left, so ETH gets pricier. The pool never asks anyone what ETH is worth: the ratio is the price.

card.title: The price is just a ratio of reserves
card.sub: No price feed inside the pool. Every trade changes the reserves, so it moves the price.

long: Price impact on x · y = k: taking Δx out of reserve x costs y · Δx / (x − Δx), so the average price paid is spot × x / (x − Δx). Buying 10% of the reserve means paying x / 0.9x ≈ 1.111, about 11.1% above the pre-trade spot price, before the fee. That gap is price impact; deeper pools (bigger reserves) give smaller impact for the same trade.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #4: Price impact on x · y = k: taking Δx out of reserve x costs y · Δx / (x − Δx), an average price of spot × x / (x − Δx). Buy 10% of the reserve and you pay x / 0.9x ≈ 1.111, ≈11.1% over spot, before the fee.

That gap is price impact. Deeper pools (bigger reserves) give smaller impact for the same trade.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #4: Big trades pay more. On a pool with x · y = k, buying 10% of one token's reserve costs you on average about 11% more per token than the price shown before the trade. That gap is "price impact".

Each token you buy makes the next one more expensive. The bigger the pool compared to your trade, the smaller this effect, which is why deep liquidity matters.

card.title: Big trades pay a hidden premium
card.sub: Buying 10% of a reserve costs about 11.1% above the pre-trade spot price, before fees.

long: Uniswap v2 charges a 0.30% (30 bps) fee on the input amount of each swap. The fee is not paid out: it stays in the reserves, so k grows with every swap and each LP share redeems for more tokens over time, in proportion to the LP's share of the pool. There is no claim step; fees compound inside the pool.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #5: Uniswap v2 charges a 0.30% (30 bps) fee on the input amount of each swap. The fee isn't paid out: it stays in the reserves, so k grows with every swap.

Each LP share is a claim on a pool that grows with fees (the token mix shifts with price), in proportion to the LP's share. No claim step: fees compound inside the pool.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #5: Each Uniswap v2 swap pays a 0.3% fee. It stays in the pool, so the pool slowly grows and the people who supplied the tokens (liquidity providers) earn it in proportion to their share.

There's nothing to claim: when you withdraw, you redeem your share of a pool that has grown with the fees, so they're already included. The fees were added to your slice all along.

card.title: Swap fees that never leave the pool
card.sub: The fee stays in the reserves, so each LP share redeems for more tokens over time.

long: Uniswap v2 has an optional protocol fee, off by default. When the feeTo address is set, 1/6 of the 0.30% swap fee (0.05% of volume) goes to it and liquidity providers keep 0.25%. It is not taken on every swap: it is collected lazily, minted as new LP shares when liquidity is added or removed.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #6: Uniswap v2 has an optional protocol fee, off by default (the "fee switch"). When the feeTo address is set, 1/6 of the 30 bps fee (0.05% of volume) goes to it and LPs keep 0.25%.

It isn't taken on every swap: it's collected lazily, minted as new LP shares when liquidity is added or removed. That saves gas on every trade.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #6: Uniswap v2 has a switch for a protocol fee, off by default. If turned on, 1/6 of the 0.3% swap fee goes to the protocol, and liquidity providers keep 0.25%.

To keep swaps cheap, the protocol's cut isn't sent at each trade. It's settled from time to time, by creating a few extra pool shares when people add or remove liquidity.

card.title: A protocol fee switch, off by default
card.sub: If turned on, 1/6 of the swap fee goes to the protocol and LPs keep 0.25%.

long: LP shares are a receipt for a slice of the pool. In Uniswap v2 the first depositor gets √(x · y) shares (geometric mean of the two amounts), so the share value does not depend on the starting price ratio; later LPs get shares in proportion to what they add. The first 1,000 units of shares (1e-15 of a share with 18 decimals) are burned to the zero address, which makes manipulating the price of one share costly.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #7: A new Uniswap v2 pool mints √(x · y) shares (geometric mean of the two amounts) to the first LP, so share value doesn't depend on the starting price ratio; later LPs get shares in proportion to what they add.

The first 1,000 units (1e-15 of a share with 18 decimals) are burned to the zero address, making share-price manipulation costly.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #7: When you add tokens to a pool you get "LP shares", a receipt for your slice. The very first depositor gets shares based on the geometric mean of both amounts, so the share value does not depend on the starting price.

A tiny amount of the first shares is also burned forever. It costs almost nothing, but it makes certain tricks to manipulate the value of one share very expensive.

card.title: How the first LP shares get counted
card.sub: The geometric mean of both deposits sets them, whatever the starting price ratio.

long: Uniswap v2 flash swaps: the pool sends the output tokens first, calls the receiver's contract, then checks at the end that x · y ≥ k with fees included. Repayment can be in either token. If it is missing, the whole transaction reverts as if nothing happened. The atomicity of the transaction plays the role of collateral.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #8: Uniswap v2 flash swaps: the pool sends the output tokens first, calls the receiver's contract, then checks at the end that x · y ≥ k, fees included. Repay in either token.

If the repayment is missing, the whole transaction reverts as if nothing happened. The atomicity of the transaction plays the role of collateral.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #8: Uniswap v2 "flash swaps": take tokens out of a pool first, use them, and pay at the end. If the payment isn't there before the transaction ends, everything is undone as if it never happened.

That lets traders, for example, buy cheap on one exchange and sell high on another without having the money upfront. The pool takes no risk: no payment, no trade.

card.title: Take the tokens first, pay at the end
card.sub: If repayment is missing when the transaction ends, everything reverts.

long: An AMM does not see outside prices. Arbitrageurs trade against it whenever y / x differs from the external market price by more than fees and gas, until it matches. So the pool's price follows the market only through arbitrage, lags it by at least the fee band, and liquidity providers bear the cost of each correction.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #9: An AMM is price-blind. Arbitrageurs trade against it whenever y / x differs from the external market price by more than fees and gas, until it matches.

So the pool's price follows the market only through arbitrage, lags it by at least the fee band, and liquidity providers bear the cost of each correction.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #9: Why do DEX prices follow the market? Arbitrage. If a pool sells ETH cheaper than elsewhere, traders buy it there until the pool's price catches up. The pool never looks at the outside price itself.

The catch: each time, the arbitrageur profits from the pool's outdated price. That profit comes from the liquidity providers, who sold ETH a bit too cheap.

card.title: Pools never look at outside prices
card.sub: Arbitrage drags the pool price toward the market, and LPs pay for each correction.

long: Impermanent loss (IL): a 50/50 x · y = k position compared with simply holding the two tokens. If the price ratio changes by a factor r, IL = 2√r / (1 + r) − 1 (derived directly from x · y = k, fees not included). It depends only on the size of the change, not its direction: the formula is symmetric in r and 1/r, so ×2 and ÷2 give the same loss.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #10: Impermanent loss (IL) of a 50/50 x · y = k position vs simply holding the two tokens, for a price ratio change r: IL = 2√r / (1 + r) − 1, derived directly from x · y = k, fees not included.

It depends only on the size of the change, not its direction: the formula is symmetric in r and 1/r, so ×2 and ÷2 give the same loss.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #10: "Impermanent loss": if prices move, a pool position ends up worth less than just holding the two tokens. It has a formula: it depends only on how much the price ratio changed, not on which way.

Why? As one token rises, the pool keeps selling it for the other. You end up with less of the winner and more of the loser than if you'd just held both.

card.title: Impermanent loss has a formula
card.sub: It depends only on how much the price ratio moved, not which way: ×2 and ÷2 hurt the same.

source: https://app.uniswap.org/whitepaper.pdf (formule dérivée de x · y = k, calcul direct)

long: Numbers from IL = 2√r / (1 + r) − 1, fees excluded: r = 1.5 gives −2.0%, r = 2 gives −5.7%, r = 3 gives −13.4%, r = 4 gives −20%, r = 5 about −25%, r = 10 gives −42.5% versus holding. Fees earned can offset it, or not. It is called impermanent only because it disappears if the price returns to the entry ratio.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #11: IL = 2√r / (1 + r) − 1, fees excluded: r = 1.5 → −2.0%, r = 2 → −5.7%, r = 3 → −13.4%, r = 4 → −20%, r = 5 ≈ −25%, r = 10 → −42.5% vs holding.

Fees earned can offset it, or not. "Impermanent" only means it vanishes if the price returns to the entry ratio.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #11: Impermanent loss in numbers: if one token's price doubles against the other, the pool position is worth about 5.7% less than holding. ×4: about 20% less. ×5: about 25% less.

The fees you earn can make up for it, or not. And "impermanent" only means the loss disappears if prices return to where you started. If they don't, it's very real.

card.title: Impermanent loss in real numbers
card.sub: A 2x price move costs about 5.7% versus holding, 4x about 20%, before fees.

source: https://app.uniswap.org/whitepaper.pdf (calcul direct à partir de la formule du post 10)

long: Loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR), from Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden and Zhang (2022), compares an LP position not to holding but to a portfolio that rebalances at CEX prices. The gap is the cost of being picked off by arbitrageurs. Unlike impermanent loss it does not reset when the price comes back: it is non-decreasing over time and grows with volatility (σ²).
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #12: Loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR, Milionis, Moallemi, Roughgarden, Zhang, 2022) compares an LP position not to holding but to a portfolio that rebalances at CEX prices. The gap is the cost of being picked off by arbitrageurs.

Unlike IL, it doesn't reset when price returns: it's non-decreasing over time and grows with volatility (σ²).
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #12: Researchers found a sharper way to measure what liquidity providers lose: compare them not to holding, but to a trader who rebalances at market prices. The gap, "LVR", is the cost of being picked off by arbitrage.

Unlike impermanent loss, it never goes away when prices come back. It only adds up, and faster when markets are volatile.

card.title: A sharper way to measure LP losses
card.sub: LVR compares LPs to a trader who rebalances at market prices. Unlike IL, it never resets.

source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.06046 (rebalancing "at CEX prices" ; ℓ = σ²P²/2·|x*′(P)| ; LVR "monotonically non-decreasing", LVH path-independent)

long: Uniswap v3 (2021) introduced concentrated liquidity: a position is only active, and only earns fees, while the price is inside its range [pa, pb]. Uniswap Labs claimed up to 4000x capital efficiency versus v2 for liquidity placed in a single 0.10% range. The same capital gives far more depth where trading happens, but the tighter the range, the more often the price leaves it.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #13: Uniswap v3 (2021) "concentrated liquidity": a position is active, and earns fees, only while the price is inside its range [pa, pb]. Uniswap Labs claimed up to 4000x capital efficiency vs v2 for liquidity in a single 0.10% range.

Same capital, far more depth where trading happens. But the tighter the range, the more often the price leaves it.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #13: Uniswap v3 (2021) let liquidity providers pick a price range. Their tokens only work, and only earn fees, while the price stays in that range. Same money, far more depth where trading happens.

A narrow range near the current price can earn a lot. But if the price moves out of it, the position stops earning until the price comes back.

card.title: Liquidity that only works in range
card.sub: Uniswap v3 positions earn fees only while the price stays inside their chosen range.

long: Uniswap v3 places a tick at every price p = 1.0001^i for integer i, so neighboring ticks are about 1 basis point (0.01%) apart. Doubling the price takes ln 2 / ln 1.0001 ≈ 6,931.8, so about 6,932 ticks. Liquidity providers choose the two ticks where their range starts and ends.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #14: Uniswap v3 places a tick at every price p = 1.0001^i, i an integer, so neighboring ticks are ≈1 basis point (0.01%) apart.

Doubling the price takes ln 2 / ln 1.0001 ≈ 6,931.8, so ≈6,932 ticks. Liquidity providers choose the two ticks where their range starts and ends.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #14: In Uniswap v3, prices move on a ladder of "ticks". Each step up is 0.01% higher than the one below. Liquidity providers pick the two steps where their range starts and ends.

To double the price, you climb about 6,932 steps. The ladder is the same for every pool, whether it trades ETH, stablecoins or anything else.

card.title: Prices climb a ladder of ticks
card.sub: Each tick is about 0.01% above the last, and doubling the price takes about 6,932 ticks.

long: Not every v3 tick can be a range edge: tick spacing restricts which ones can be initialized. At launch: spacing 10 for the 0.05% fee tier (about 0.10% between usable ticks), 60 for 0.30%, 200 for 1%. Fewer initializable ticks means fewer tick crossings during a swap, so less gas. Low-fee pools get a finer grid, high-fee pools a coarser one.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #15: Not every v3 tick can be a range edge: tick spacing restricts which can be initialized. At launch: 10 for the 0.05% fee tier (≈0.10% between usable ticks), 60 for 0.30%, 200 for 1%.

Fewer initializable ticks means fewer tick crossings during a swap, so less gas. Low-fee pools get a finer grid, high-fee pools a coarser one.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #15: In Uniswap v3, not every tick can be a range edge. Low-fee pools use a finer grid, high-fee pools a coarser one, which keeps swaps cheaper to run.

Each time a swap crosses a range edge, it costs extra gas. Fewer possible edges means fewer crossings. Stable pairs get fine precision, volatile pairs a coarser ladder.

card.title: Not every tick can be a range edge
card.sub: Low-fee pools get a finer grid, high-fee pools a coarser one, which keeps swaps cheaper.

long: Uniswap v3 does not store the price but its square root, sqrtPriceX96: √P as a fixed-point uint160 with 96 fractional bits. With liquidity L, virtual reserves are x = L / √P and y = L · √P, so within a tick a swap moves √P linearly with Δy and no square root has to be computed on-chain. The swap math becomes simpler and cheaper.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #16: Uniswap v3 stores not the price but sqrtPriceX96: √P as a fixed-point uint160 with 96 fractional bits.

With liquidity L, virtual reserves are x = L / √P and y = L · √P, so within a tick a swap moves √P linearly with Δy and no square root is computed on-chain. Simpler, cheaper swap math.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #16: Uniswap v3 doesn't store the price itself. It stores the square root of the price, because the swap math gets simpler and cheaper with it.

Computing square roots on Ethereum is expensive. By storing the root directly, most swaps only need additions and multiplications, which saves gas on every trade.

card.title: Uniswap v3 stores the square root of price
card.sub: Within a tick, swaps move √P linearly, so no square root is computed on-chain.

long: When the price leaves a v3 position's range, the position earns no fees and holds 100% of one token: the one that fell in relative price. Placing a single token in a range above or below the current price makes it convert as the price crosses the range: a range order, similar to a limit order, filled on average at √(pa · pb), the geometric mean of the bounds.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #17: Out of range, a v3 position earns no fees and holds 100% of one token: the one that fell in relative price.

Place a single token in a range above or below the current price and it converts as the price crosses the range: a "range order", similar to a limit order, filled on average at √(pa · pb), the geometric mean of the bounds.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #17: A Uniswap v3 position that the price leaves earns nothing and ends up 100% in one token: the one that went down in price. That's also how "range orders" work, a bit like a limit order.

Put only ETH in a range above today's price: if the price rises through it, your ETH gets sold for USDC along the way, like a sell order.

card.title: When the price leaves your range
card.sub: The position stops earning and ends up fully in one token. That is how range orders work.

long: In Uniswap v2 all LP shares are identical and fungible. In v3 each position has its own range [pa, pb] and fee history, so positions are not fungible. The core contracts track them per position, and the periphery represents each one as an ERC-721 NFT. Getting fungible LP tokens back requires a separate wrapper contract.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #18: In Uniswap v2, all LP shares are identical and fungible. In v3, each position has its own range [pa, pb] and fee history, so positions aren't fungible.

The core contracts track them per position, and the periphery represents each one as an ERC-721 NFT. Getting fungible LP tokens back requires a separate wrapper contract.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #18: In Uniswap v2, every liquidity share is the same, like a coin. In v3, each position has its own range, so each one is a unique token: an NFT.

Two people with the same amount in the same pool can hold very different positions. That's why they can't simply be swapped one for one, like coins.

card.title: Why v3 positions became NFTs
card.sub: Each position has its own range and fee history, so no two are interchangeable.

long: Uniswap v2 built-in oracle: each pair keeps a cumulative sum of price × seconds, updated at the start of each block before the first trade, with prices stored as UQ112.112 fixed-point. Read the accumulator at two times and divide the difference by the elapsed time to get a time-weighted average price (TWAP) over any window, much harder to manipulate than a single moment's price.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #19: Uniswap v2 built-in oracle: each pair keeps a cumulative sum of price × seconds, updated at the start of each block before the first trade, with prices stored as UQ112.112 fixed-point.

Read it at two times and divide the difference by elapsed time: a TWAP over any window, much harder to manipulate than a single moment's price.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #19: Other apps need prices too. Uniswap v2 records a running total of the price over time, so anyone can compute an average price over the last hour or day, which is much harder to fake than one moment.

Recording happens before the first trade of each block, so a trader can't push the price and record it in the same breath.

card.title: A price oracle built into every pair
card.sub: A running total of price over time lets anyone compute a time-weighted average price.

long: Uniswap v3 changed the oracle: it accumulates the tick (log base 1.0001 of the price) per second, so a TWAP is a geometric mean, 1.0001^(Δacc / Δt). Any app can query an average over a past window in one call, and a pool can store up to 65,536 checkpoints, about 9 days of history on Ethereum at launch.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #20: Uniswap v3 accumulates the tick (log base 1.0001 of the price) per second, so a TWAP is a geometric mean: 1.0001^(Δacc / Δt).

Any app can query an average over a past window in one call, and a pool can store up to 65,536 checkpoints, about 9 days of history on Ethereum at launch.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #20: Uniswap v3 upgraded its built-in price feed: any app can ask for an average price over a past window in one call, and the pool can keep a long history of checkpoints.

Up to about 9 days of history on Ethereum at launch. In v2, apps had to store snapshots themselves; v3 keeps them inside the pool.

card.title: Averages over any past window, one call
card.sub: Uniswap v3 accumulates the tick per second and can keep about 9 days of checkpoints.

long: A spot price y / x read in the middle of a transaction can be pushed by one swap and restored by the next, inside the same transaction, for little cost beyond fees. That is why it should never be used as a trusted price. A TWAP forces an attacker to hold the distorted price across several blocks, paying arbitrage losses each block; serious protocols use averages or external oracle feeds.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #21: A spot price y / x read mid-transaction can be pushed by one swap and restored by the next, in the same tx, for little cost beyond fees. It should never be trusted as a price.

A TWAP forces an attacker to hold the distorted price across several blocks, paying arbitrage losses each block. Serious protocols use averages or external oracle feeds.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #21: Never use a DEX's current price as a trusted price. Someone with enough money can push it, use it, and put it back, all within a single transaction.

That's why serious protocols use averages over time or outside price feeds. To fake an average, an attacker would have to hold a wrong price for many blocks, losing money to arbitrage the whole time.

card.title: Never trust a price one swap can move
card.sub: A spot price can be pushed and restored within one transaction. Averages resist that.

long: bZx, February 15, 2020, one of the first well-known flash-loan attacks, in a single transaction: a 10,000 ETH flash loan from dYdX; 1,300 ETH funded a 5x short on bZx whose large ETH to WBTC swap went through Uniswap and pushed WBTC up. In the same tx the attacker had posted 5,500 ETH as collateral on Compound and borrowed 112 WBTC, and sold those 112 WBTC on Uniswap for about 6,800 ETH. bZx trusted a price that one trade could move.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #22: bZx, Feb 15, 2020, one tx: a 10,000 ETH flash loan from dYdX; 1,300 ETH funded a 5x short on bZx whose big ETH→WBTC swap went through Uniswap, pumping WBTC.

The attacker had posted 5,500 ETH as collateral on Compound and borrowed 112 WBTC, then sold them on Uniswap for ≈6,871 ETH. bZx trusted a price one trade could move.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #22: February 15, 2020: one of the first famous DeFi attacks. The attacker borrowed 10,000 ETH for a few seconds, pushed up a price on Uniswap, and profited from a lending protocol (bZx) that trusted it.

Everything happened in a single transaction: borrow, manipulate, profit, repay. The flaw wasn't in the loan, but in trusting a price one big trade could move.

card.title: The bZx attack in a single transaction
card.sub: A flash loan pushed WBTC up on Uniswap, and bZx trusted a price that one trade could move.

long: Mango Markets, October 11, 2022: 483M MNGO perpetuals were bought at $0.0382 between two accounts of the attacker, then the MNGO spot price was pushed to $0.91, more than 20x. The unrealized profit counted as collateral, and about $116M was borrowed out. The oracle reported the real market price; the problem was a market too thin to resist manipulation.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #23: Mango Markets, Oct 11, 2022: 483M MNGO perps were bought at $0.0382 between two of the attacker's accounts, then MNGO spot was pushed to $0.91, more than 20x.

The unrealized PnL counted as collateral and ≈$116M was borrowed out. The oracle reported the real market price; the market was too thin to resist manipulation.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #23: October 11, 2022: a trader on Mango Markets pushed the price of the thin MNGO token up more than 20x, used the inflated position as collateral, and borrowed out about $116M.

The price feed was honest: MNGO really did trade that high, briefly. The problem was a market so small that one person could move it, and a protocol that lent against it.

card.title: Honest oracle, thin market
card.sub: MNGO was pushed up more than 20x, and the inflated position was used as collateral.

long: Uniswap v4 launched on January 31, 2025, on 10 networks. Its main design change is a singleton: one PoolManager contract holds every pool, instead of one contract per pool. Creating a pool becomes a state update rather than a contract deployment, reported as about 99.9% cheaper than in v3, and multi-hop swaps no longer move tokens between separate pool contracts.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #24: Uniswap v4 (Jan 31, 2025, 10 networks) uses a singleton: one PoolManager holds every pool, instead of one contract per pool.

A new pool is a state update, not a contract deploy: reported ≈99.9% cheaper to create than in v3. Multi-hop swaps no longer move tokens between separate pool contracts.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #24: Uniswap v4 went live on January 31, 2025 on 10 networks. Big change: every pool now lives in one single contract instead of one contract per pool. Creating a pool got about 99.9% cheaper than in v3.

Swaps through several pools also got cheaper: the tokens stay inside one contract instead of being sent from pool to pool at each step.

card.title: One contract to hold every pool
card.sub: Uniswap v4 made creating a pool a state update instead of a new contract deployment.

long: Uniswap v4 hooks are external contracts a pool can attach, called at fixed points such as beforeSwap / afterSwap and before/after adding or removing liquidity. They allow dynamic fees, custom pricing logic or liquidity rewards without forking Uniswap. Which hooks are active is encoded in bits of the hook contract's address, so the pool knows which calls to make.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #25: v4 hooks are external contracts a pool can attach, called at fixed points like beforeSwap / afterSwap and before/after adding or removing liquidity. They allow dynamic fees, custom pricing or LP rewards without forking Uniswap.

Which hooks are active is encoded in bits of the hook contract's address, so the pool knows which calls to make.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #25: Uniswap v4 "hooks" let a pool's creator plug in their own code that runs at set moments, like before or after a swap. That allows dynamic fees, custom pricing curves or liquidity rewards without forking Uniswap.

The flip side: a pool is only as safe as its hook. Before using a pool with a custom hook, it's worth knowing who wrote it.

card.title: Plug custom code into a pool
card.sub: Hooks run before or after swaps, enabling dynamic fees or custom pricing without a fork.

long: Flash accounting in Uniswap v4: during an unlock, PoolManager records a running delta of tokens owed per caller instead of transferring tokens at each step of a multi-step trade. Every delta must be settled to zero before unlock returns, or the transaction reverts. The deltas are kept in transient storage (EIP-1153), which is cleared at the end of the transaction.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #26: v4 "flash accounting": during an unlock, PoolManager records a running delta of tokens owed per caller instead of transferring tokens at each step of a multi-step trade.

Every delta must be settled to zero before unlock returns, or the tx reverts. The deltas live in transient storage (EIP-1153), cleared at the end of the transaction.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #26: In Uniswap v4, a multi-step trade doesn't move tokens at every step. The contract just keeps a running tab, and only the final balance must be settled before the transaction ends.

Fewer token transfers means less gas. And if anything is still owed at the end, the whole transaction is cancelled, so the pools can't be left short.

card.title: A running tab instead of transfers
card.sub: Uniswap v4 tracks what each caller owes, and every balance must settle to zero.

long: Why not x + y = k? Constant sum gives zero slippage at a fixed price of 1, but as soon as the external price drifts (a depeg), arbitrage drains one side completely. Constant product can never be emptied, but has high slippage even near 1:1. Curve's StableSwap blends the two curves.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #27: Why not x + y = k? Constant sum gives zero slippage at a fixed price of 1, but as soon as the external price drifts (a depeg), arbitrage drains one side completely.

Constant product can never be emptied, but has high slippage even near 1:1. Curve's StableSwap blends the two curves to get the best of both.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #27: Why not use "x + y = k" instead of x · y = k? Price would never move, which sounds great, until arbitrage drains one token completely the moment its outside price drifts.

x · y = k never runs dry, but prices move a lot even for coins that should be equal. Curve found a middle path between the two.

card.title: The flaw in a flat price curve
card.sub: Constant sum has zero slippage until a depeg lets arbitrage drain one side completely.

long: Curve StableSwap, paper by Michael Egorov, November 2019, for assets meant to trade at par like dollar stablecoins. Invariant: A·nⁿ·Σxᵢ + D = A·D·nⁿ + Dⁿ⁺¹ / (nⁿ·Πxᵢ), where D is the total amount when all coins are at equal price. Near balance it behaves like constant sum (very flat prices around 1:1), far from balance like constant product, so the pool still cannot be fully emptied.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #28: Curve StableSwap (Michael Egorov, Nov 2019), for assets meant to trade at par: A·nⁿ·Σxᵢ + D = A·D·nⁿ + Dⁿ⁺¹ / (nⁿ·Πxᵢ), D being the total when all coins are at par.

Near balance it acts like constant sum (very flat prices around 1:1), far from it like constant product, so the pool still can't be fully emptied.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #28: Curve's StableSwap (paper by Michael Egorov, November 2019) is built for tokens that should be worth the same, like two dollar stablecoins: very flat prices near 1:1, but the pool still can't be fully emptied.

In a deep pool, swapping $1M of one stablecoin for another barely moves the price. But if one coin loses its peg, the curve bends so the pool can't be fully emptied, though LPs end up holding mostly the weaker coin.

card.title: A curve built for coins at par
card.sub: StableSwap is flat like constant sum near balance, and like constant product far from it.

long: StableSwap's amplification coefficient A sets the leverage on the constant-sum part. The effective leverage equals A when the pool is perfectly balanced and falls toward 0 as it becomes imbalanced; A → 0 gives constant product. Higher A means flatter prices around 1:1, suited to coins that hold their peg; lower A behaves more like Uniswap. The paper uses A = 100 for its slippage calculation.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #29: StableSwap's amplification coefficient A sets the leverage on the constant-sum part: effective leverage equals A when the pool is balanced and fades toward 0 as it tilts; A → 0 gives constant product.

Higher A means flatter prices around 1:1, for coins that hold their peg. The paper's slippage example uses A = 100.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #29: Curve pools have a dial called "A". Turn it up and prices stay flatter around 1:1, good for coins that really hold their peg. Turn it down and the pool behaves more like Uniswap.

The dial matters most in a crisis: a high A is efficient on calm days, but leaves less protection if one of the coins starts to slip.

card.title: The dial that flattens Curve prices
card.sub: Higher A means flatter prices around 1:1. Lower A behaves more like Uniswap.

long: Balancer generalizes the constant product: a weighted pool keeps Π Bᵢ^wᵢ constant, with balances Bᵢ and weights summing to 1, for several tokens and any weights such as 80/20. Spot price of token o in units of token i is (Bᵢ / wᵢ) / (Bₒ / wₒ). Trades and arbitrage keep the pool's value split along the weights. With two tokens at 50/50 it reduces to Uniswap's x · y = k.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #30: Balancer weighted pools generalize constant product: Π Bᵢ^wᵢ = constant, balances Bᵢ, weights summing to 1, for several tokens and any weights like 80/20.

Spot price of token o in units of token i: (Bᵢ / wᵢ) / (Bₒ / wₒ). Arbitrage keeps value split along the weights. Two tokens at 50/50 give Uniswap's x · y = k.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #30: Balancer generalizes Uniswap: a pool can hold several tokens with any weights, like 80% of one and 20% of another. Trades and arbitrage keep the pool's value split along those weights.

It works like a self-rebalancing index fund: when one token rises, the pool sells some of it to keep the weights, and traders pay fees for the privilege.

card.title: Uniswap's formula with any weights
card.sub: Balancer pools hold several tokens and keep their value split along fixed weights.

long: DeFi lending has no credit check, so loans are overcollateralized. On Aave each collateral asset has a maximum loan-to-value (LTV), how much can be borrowed against it, and a liquidation threshold, which the contracts require to be at least the LTV and which sets when a position can be liquidated. The gap between them is the safety margin when the loan is opened. Lock $10,000 of ETH and you can borrow less than $10,000.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #31: DeFi lending has no credit check, so regular loans are overcollateralized. On Aave, each collateral asset has a max loan-to-value (LTV) and a liquidation threshold, never lower, that sets when a position can be liquidated.

The gap between the two is the safety margin when the loan is opened.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #31: DeFi lending has no credit check, so regular loans are backed by more collateral than it borrows. Lock $10,000 of ETH and you can borrow less than $10,000 of stablecoins, never more.

How much less depends on the asset: riskier collateral lets you borrow a smaller share. And a second, higher limit decides when your loan can be liquidated.

card.title: No credit check, so more collateral
card.sub: Lock $10,000 of ETH and you can borrow less than $10,000, never more.

long: Aave health factor = Σ(collateral value × liquidation threshold) / total debt. Above 1 the position is safe; below 1 anyone can repay part of the debt and take collateral at a discount. Example: $10,000 collateral at an 80% threshold with $7,000 debt gives 8,000 / 7,000 ≈ 1.14. A 12.5% drop in collateral value (to $8,750) brings it to exactly 1.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #32: Aave health factor = Σ(collateral value × liquidation threshold) / total debt. Above 1, safe; below 1, anyone can repay part of the debt and take collateral at a discount.

Example: $10,000 collateral at an 80% threshold with $7,000 debt gives 8,000 / 7,000 ≈ 1.14. A 12.5% collateral drop (to $8,750) brings it to exactly 1.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #32: Aave sums up a loan's safety in one number, the "health factor". Above 1 you're fine. Below 1, anyone can repay part or all of your loan and take some of your collateral at a discount.

Example, with an 80% liquidation threshold: borrow $7,000 against $10,000 of ETH and your health factor is about 1.14. A 12.5% drop in ETH is enough to put you at the edge.

card.title: One number that decides liquidation
card.sub: Above a health factor of 1 a loan is safe. Below 1, anyone can liquidate part of it.

long: Aave v3.3 close factor (a governance parameter, can change): if the health factor is above 0.95 (and below 1) and the collateral and debt reserves being liquidated are each worth at least $2,000, a liquidation can repay up to 50% of the user's total debt. If HF ≤ 0.95, or either of those reserves is under $2,000, up to 100% of that debt reserve can be repaid.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #33: Aave v3.3 close factor (a governance parameter): if 0.95 < HF < 1 and the liquidated collateral and debt reserves are each worth ≥ $2,000, one liquidation can repay up to 50% of the debt.

If HF ≤ 0.95, or either reserve is under $2,000, up to 100% of that debt reserve can be repaid.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #33: On Aave, a liquidation usually doesn't wipe the whole loan at once. A liquidator can repay up to half of it, unless the position is very unhealthy or small, in which case all of it can go.

The idea: a loan just below the line gets a partial fix, which may bring it back to safety. A badly broken or tiny loan is cleared in one go.

card.title: Liquidations usually take half
card.sub: Up to half the debt can be repaid, or all of it if the position is very unhealthy.

long: Why liquidators act: Aave sets a liquidation bonus per collateral asset. The liquidator repays debt D and receives collateral worth D × (1 + bonus). Bots compete for this bonus, which is what keeps the protocol solvent when prices fall; for the borrower, the bonus is the cost of letting the loan go bad.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #34: Aave sets a liquidation bonus per collateral asset: the liquidator repays debt D and receives collateral worth D × (1 + bonus).

Bots compete for this bonus, which is what keeps the protocol solvent when prices fall. For the borrower, the bonus is the cost of letting the loan go bad.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #34: Why would anyone liquidate you? Because it pays: the liquidator repays some of your debt and receives your collateral worth a bit more than what they paid. That bonus is the cost you pay for letting your loan go bad.

Bots watch every loan, all the time, racing to be first. Harsh for borrowers, but it's what keeps lenders' money safe when prices crash.

card.title: Why anyone would liquidate you
card.sub: Liquidators get collateral worth more than the debt repaid. The bonus keeps Aave solvent.

long: DeFi lending rates come from a formula, not a banker. Utilization U = borrows / (cash + borrows − reserves). Compound's jump rate model raises the borrow rate slowly with U up to a kink, then steeply above it, pushing borrowers to repay and keeping cash available for lenders who want to withdraw.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #35: DeFi lending rates come from a formula. Utilization U = borrows / (cash + borrows − reserves).

Compound's jump rate model raises the borrow rate slowly with U up to a "kink", then steeply above it, pushing borrowers to repay and keeping cash available for lenders who want to withdraw.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #35: Interest rates in DeFi lending aren't set by a banker. They follow a formula based on how much of the pool is already lent out. The more it's borrowed, the more borrowing costs.

Past a certain point, rates jump sharply. That's on purpose: it pushes borrowers to repay so there's always cash left for lenders who want their money back.

card.title: Interest rates set by a formula
card.sub: Borrowing costs rise slowly with utilization, then steeply above a kink.

long: In Compound v2, supply rate = borrow rate × utilization × (1 − reserve factor). Lenders earn less than borrowers pay because part of the pool sits unlent and the protocol keeps a cut for reserves. Example: 80% utilization, 5% borrow rate, 10% reserve factor gives 5% × 0.8 × 0.9 = 3.6% for lenders.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #36: In Compound v2, supply rate = borrow rate × utilization × (1 − reserve factor). Lenders earn less than borrowers pay: part of the pool sits unlent, and the protocol keeps a cut for reserves.

Example: 80% utilization, 5% borrow rate, 10% reserve factor gives 5% × 0.8 × 0.9 = 3.6% for lenders.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #36: Lenders earn less than borrowers pay. Part of the pool sits unlent, so its interest is spread over everyone, and the protocol keeps a cut for its reserves.

Example: borrowers pay 5%, 80% of the pool is lent out, and the protocol keeps 10% of interest. Lenders then earn about 3.6%.

card.title: Lenders earn less than borrowers pay
card.sub: Part of the pool sits unlent, and the protocol keeps a cut for its reserves.

long: Two ways a deposit receipt grows. Aave aTokens rebase: balanceOf() returns the scaled balance × the liquidity index, so the number of tokens in the wallet rises over time. Compound v2 cTokens do not rebase: the count stays fixed and the exchange rate from cToken to the underlying asset rises instead.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #37: Two ways a deposit receipt grows. Aave aTokens rebase: balanceOf() returns the scaled balance × the liquidity index, so the token count in the wallet rises over time.

Compound v2 cTokens don't rebase: the count stays fixed, and the exchange rate from cToken to the underlying asset rises instead.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #37: Your deposit receipt can grow in two ways. On Aave, the number of receipt tokens in your wallet goes up. On Compound v2, the number stays the same but each one is worth more.

Same result, different display. It matters for apps: a balance that changes by itself can confuse software that expects it to stay put.

card.title: Two ways a deposit receipt grows
card.sub: Aave adds tokens to your wallet. Compound v2 keeps the count fixed and raises their value.

long: Aave v3 flashLoan(): the pool sends the funds with no collateral, the borrower's executeOperation() runs, then the pool pulls back amount + premium. Premium: currently 0.05% on Aave V3 (the Pool contract's initial default was 0.09%), changeable by governance. If repayment fails, the whole transaction reverts, so the loan only exists within one transaction.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #38: Aave v3 flashLoan(): the pool sends funds with no collateral, the borrower's executeOperation() runs, then the pool pulls back amount + premium. The premium (0.05%) is set by governance.

If repayment fails, the whole tx reverts, so the loan only exists within one transaction.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #38: A flash loan lends you millions with no collateral, for one transaction only. If the money isn't back, plus a fee, by the end of that transaction, the blockchain cancels everything, as if the loan never happened.

The lender takes no risk. It's used for arbitrage, refinancing, or closing loans, and, as we'll see, also for attacks.

card.title: Millions lent for one transaction
card.sub: No collateral needed. If funds plus fee are not back by the end, everything reverts.

long: Euler Finance, March 13, 2023: about $197M taken. Flash loans supplied the capital to exploit a flaw in a recently added function; the flash loan was repaid in the same transaction, Euler's lenders were not. The point: flash loans do not create bugs, they scale them. A flaw that needs $100M of capital no longer needs a whale, only gas and the loan fee.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #39: Euler Finance, Mar 13, 2023: ≈$197M taken. Flash loans supplied the capital to exploit a flaw in a recently added function; the loan was repaid in the same tx.

Euler's lenders were left short at the time; most funds were returned in April 2023. Flash loans don't create bugs, they scale them: a flaw needing $100M of capital no longer needs a whale, only gas and the loan fee.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #39: Flash loans don't create bugs, they scale them. A flaw that needs $100M to exploit used to need a whale. With a flash loan, anyone who can pay the gas and the fee can try it.

Euler Finance learned it in March 2023: about $197M taken through a flaw in a new function. The flash loan was paid back. Euler's lenders, at the time, weren't, though most funds came back in April 2023.

card.title: Flash loans scale bugs, not create them
card.sub: A flaw that needs $100M of capital no longer needs a whale, only gas and the loan fee.

long: DAI began as a loan. A Maker vault locks collateral such as ETH and mints new DAI against it, as long as the vault stays above the minimum collateral ratio of its vault type. The debt accrues a stability fee; repaying burns the DAI and frees the collateral. If the ratio falls below the minimum, the vault is liquidated and its collateral auctioned to cover the debt.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #40: DAI began as a loan. A Maker vault locks collateral such as ETH and mints DAI against it, as long as it stays above its vault type's minimum collateral ratio. Debt accrues a stability fee; repaying burns the DAI.

Below the ratio, the vault is liquidated and its collateral auctioned to cover the debt.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #40: DAI started as a loan: you lock ETH in a Maker vault and mint new DAI against it. Pay the DAI back plus a fee and you get your ETH. If ETH falls too far, the vault is auctioned.

So DAI was originally designed to be backed by more than a dollar of crypto per DAI. Today, other assets such as USDC also back it.

card.title: DAI started as a loan
card.sub: Lock ETH in a Maker vault, mint DAI against it, and repay to get the collateral back.

long: Black Thursday, March 12-13, 2020: ETH crashed and Ethereum gas prices spiked. Maker's oracle price updates were delayed and keeper bots, not built for such gas prices, stopped bidding. Bids of 0 DAI won auctions: 62,892.93 ETH, about $8.32M, went to four addresses. The design assumed bidders could always get a transaction in.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #41: Black Thursday, Mar 12-13, 2020: ETH crashed and gas spiked. Maker's oracle updates were delayed, and keeper bots, not built for such gas prices, stopped bidding.

Bids of 0 DAI won auctions: 62,892.93 ETH, ≈$8.32M, went to four addresses. The design assumed bidders could always get a tx in.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #41: March 12, 2020, "Black Thursday": ETH crashed, Ethereum got congested, and few bots could bid in Maker's liquidation auctions. Some auctions were won for 0 DAI: about $8.3M of ETH taken for free.

The auctions worked as coded. They just assumed there would always be bidders able to get a transaction through, and on that day there weren't.

card.title: Auctions won for nothing on Black Thursday
card.sub: Gas spikes stopped keeper bots from bidding, and about $8.3M of ETH went for free.

long: Liquity v1 lets users borrow LUSD against ETH with a minimum collateral ratio of 110%, a minimum debt of 2,000 LUSD, and a one-off borrowing fee from 0.5% to 5%. Redemptions let anyone swap LUSD for ETH at face value ($1 of ETH per LUSD), taken from the Troves with the lowest collateral ratio first. That gives LUSD a hard price floor near $1.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #42: Liquity v1: borrow LUSD against ETH with a 110% minimum collateral ratio, a 2,000 LUSD minimum debt and a one-off fee of 0.5% to 5%.

Redemptions let anyone swap LUSD for $1 of ETH minus a fee (at least 0.5%), taken from the Troves with the lowest ratio first. Arbitrage then creates a price floor near $1.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #42: Liquity lets you borrow its LUSD stablecoin against ETH with only 110% collateral. The trick: anyone can swap 1 LUSD for $1 worth of ETH, minus a small fee, from the riskiest loans, which holds the price near $1.

If LUSD trades at $0.97, traders buy it and redeem it for $1 of ETH. That buying pushes the price back up, with no company in charge.

card.title: A hard floor near one dollar
card.sub: Anyone can redeem 1 LUSD for $1 of ETH, taken from the riskiest Troves first.

long: Three stablecoin designs, three failure modes. Fiat-backed (USDC): the issuer holds cash and redeems it, custody risk. Crypto-collateralized (DAI, LUSD): overcollateralized on-chain vaults, liquidation risk. Algorithmic: mint and burn against a volatile token, reflexivity risk, as UST showed.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #43: Three stablecoin designs, three failure modes. Fiat-backed (USDC): the issuer holds cash and redeems it, custody risk. Crypto-collateralized (DAI, LUSD): overcollateralized on-chain vaults, liquidation risk.

Algorithmic: mint and burn against a volatile token, reflexivity risk, as UST showed.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #43: Not all stablecoins work the same way. Some hold dollars in a bank (USDC), some are backed by crypto locked on-chain (DAI, LUSD), and some tried to hold the peg with code alone. Each fails in a different way.

The bank can fail, the crypto can crash too fast, or the code can spiral. Knowing which kind you hold tells you which risk you carry.

card.title: Three stablecoin designs, three risks
card.sub: Fiat-backed: custody risk. Crypto-backed: liquidation risk. Algorithmic: reflexivity.

long: USDC, March 11, 2023: Circle disclosed that $3.3B of about $40B of reserves (about 8%) was at the failed Silicon Valley Bank. USDC traded at about $0.877. DAI, heavily backed by USDC at the time, followed it down. Even a fully cash-backed stablecoin carries custody risk, and that risk passes to everything built on it.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #44: USDC, Mar 11, 2023: Circle disclosed that $3.3B of ≈$40B of reserves (≈8%) sat at the failed Silicon Valley Bank. USDC traded ≈$0.877.

DAI, heavily backed by USDC at the time, followed it down. Even a fully cash-backed stablecoin carries custody risk, and it passes to everything built on it.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #44: Even a fully cash-backed stablecoin can wobble. In March 2023, Circle said $3.3B of USDC's reserves were stuck at the failing Silicon Valley Bank. USDC traded around $0.88 for a while.

DAI dropped too, because much of its backing was USDC. The peg returned once US authorities guaranteed the bank's deposits. Risks travel along the chain.

card.title: When cash backing sits at a failed bank
card.sub: Circle had $3.3B of USDC reserves at Silicon Valley Bank, and DAI followed USDC down.

long: Terra UST had no cash backing. Its mechanism: burn 1 UST to mint about $1 of LUNA (minus a spread), and the reverse. Defending the peg dilutes LUNA, so a run becomes a death spiral: more redemptions, more LUNA minted, lower LUNA price. The run started on May 7, 2022; LUNA supply went from about 1 billion to about 6 trillion units and its price from about $80 to almost zero within days.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #45: Terra UST had no cash backing. Burn 1 UST to mint ≈$1 of LUNA (minus a spread), and the reverse. Peg defense dilutes LUNA, so a run becomes a death spiral: more redemptions, more LUNA, lower LUNA price.

The run began May 7, 2022; LUNA supply went from ≈1B to ≈6T units and its price from ≈$80 to almost zero in days.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #45: Terra's UST had no cash behind it. The promise: 1 UST could be swapped for about $1 worth of the LUNA token. When people rushed to exit in May 2022, LUNA was printed so fast it lost almost all its value.

The more people left, the more LUNA was created, and the less each one was worth. In a few days, LUNA went from about $80 to almost nothing.

card.title: How a peg defense became a death spiral
card.sub: Each UST redeemed minted more LUNA, and its price fell from about $80 to almost zero.

source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/terra-money/classic-core/main/x/market/spec/01_concepts.md (mécanisme de swap UST↔LUNA, spread) ; https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/2023/05/22/anatomy-of-a-run-the-terra-luna-crash/ (Liu, Makarov, Schoar : run à partir du 7 mai 2022, dilution, LUNA de 1 Md à 6 000 Md d'unités, de $80 à presque 0 en trois jours)

long: A peg is only as tight as its redemption path. Below $1, arbitrageurs buy the coin and redeem it for $1 of backing; above $1, they mint and sell. Maker's PSM swaps USDC and DAI 1:1 plus a set fee, which boxes DAI's price between those fees. Without a cheap redemption path there is no hard floor, only a softer market price.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #46: A peg is only as tight as its redemption path. Below $1, arbitrageurs buy and redeem for $1 of backing; above $1, they mint and sell.

Maker's PSM swaps USDC ↔ DAI 1:1 plus a set fee, which boxes DAI's price between those fees. No cheap redemption path means no hard floor, just a softer market price.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #46: How a stablecoin peg is held in practice: if it trades under $1, someone buys it cheap and redeems it for $1 of backing. If it trades above $1, someone mints new coins and sells them. Arbitrage does the work.

The cheaper and easier that swap is, the tighter the peg. When redeeming is slow or impossible, the price can drift much further.

card.title: A peg is only as tight as its exits
card.sub: Below $1, arbitrageurs redeem for backing. Above $1, they mint and sell.

long: ERC-4626 is the tokenized vault standard: deposit tokens, receive shares worth a slice of everything the vault holds. Deposit: shares = assets × totalSupply / totalAssets. Redeem: assets = shares × totalAssets / totalSupply. When the vault earns, totalAssets rises and each share is worth more. The spec says rounding should favor the vault, not the user.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #47: ERC-4626, the tokenized vault standard: deposit tokens, receive shares worth a slice of everything the vault holds. Deposit: shares = assets × totalSupply / totalAssets. Redeem: assets = shares × totalAssets / totalSupply.

When the vault earns, totalAssets rises and each share is worth more. The spec says rounding should favor the vault.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #47: A DeFi "vault" works like a fund: you deposit tokens and get shares. Your shares are worth your slice of everything the vault holds, so when the vault earns, every share is worth a bit more.

A common standard (ERC-4626) means any app can plug into any vault the same way. Rounding always goes slightly in the vault's favor, to protect other depositors.

card.title: A vault works like a fund
card.sub: Shares are a slice of everything the vault holds, so they gain value when it earns.

long: ERC-4626 inflation attack on an empty vault: the attacker deposits 1 wei for 1 share, then donates D tokens directly, so 1 share is worth D + 1. A victim depositing less than that receives 0 shares through rounding, and the attacker's share captures the deposit. OpenZeppelin's fix uses virtual shares and assets (a decimals offset) to defend against it.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #48: ERC-4626 inflation attack on an empty vault: the attacker deposits 1 wei for 1 share, then donates D tokens directly, so 1 share is worth D + 1.

A victim depositing less than that gets 0 shares by rounding, and the attacker's share captures the deposit. OpenZeppelin's fix: virtual shares and assets (a decimals offset).
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #48: A new, empty vault can be a trap. The first depositor can buy one tiny share, then send tokens straight in to inflate its value. The next person's deposit then rounds down to zero shares, and the first one takes it.

Modern vault code adds "virtual" shares from the start, which makes this trick unprofitable for the attacker.

card.title: The empty vault trap
card.sub: A donation inflates the first share, so the next deposit rounds down to zero shares.

long: Perpetual futures never expire, so a funding payment keeps them near the index price. When the perp trades above the index, longs pay shorts; below it, shorts pay longs. The rate mostly tracks the perp's premium over the index. On dYdX v4 funding is computed and paid every hour.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #49: Perpetual futures never expire, so a funding payment keeps them near the index price. Perp above the index: longs pay shorts; below it: shorts pay longs.

The rate mostly tracks the perp's premium over the index. On dYdX v4, funding is computed and paid every hour.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #49: Perpetual futures never expire. To keep their price close to the real one, traders on the crowded side pay the other side a small fee at regular intervals: the "funding rate".

When everyone is betting on a rise, longs pay shorts. That makes shorting more attractive, which pulls the price back toward the real market.

card.title: Futures that never expire
card.sub: Funding flows from the crowded side to the other, and dYdX v4 pays it every hour.

long: Ethena's USDe is a synthetic dollar built from a trade, not from cash: it holds mostly crypto collateral plus some stablecoins, and opens short futures of about the same notional size, so net price exposure (delta) is about zero. Part of its revenue comes from funding and the basis on that hedge. It is not a fiat-backed coin and its risks are different.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #50: Ethena's USDe is a synthetic dollar built from a trade, not from cash: mostly crypto collateral plus some stablecoins, hedged with short futures of about the same notional, so net delta ≈ 0.

Part of its revenue comes from funding and the basis on that hedge. Not a fiat-backed coin: its risks are different.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #50: Some "synthetic dollars" are built from trades, not cash. Ethena's USDe holds mostly crypto and opens an equal short position against it, so a price drop on one side is offset by a gain on the other.

The yield comes partly from funding payments on those shorts. If funding turns negative or an exchange fails, the risks look nothing like a bank-backed coin's.

card.title: A dollar built from a trade
card.sub: USDe holds crypto and shorts an equal amount, so its net price exposure is about zero.

source: https://docs.ethena.fi/overview/how-usde-works (short futures "in approximately the same notional size") ; https://docs.ethena.fi/protocol-overview/risks/funding-risk (revenu du funding et de la base)

long: Chainlink Data Feeds aggregate prices from many sources and post them on-chain, but only when the price moves beyond a deviation threshold or when the heartbeat (maximum time since the last update) expires, whichever comes first. Between updates, contracts read the last posted value, so an on-chain price can be slightly stale by design.
tech:
#DeFi Mechanics #51: Chainlink Data Feeds aggregate prices from many sources and post them on-chain, but only when the price moves beyond a deviation threshold or when the heartbeat (max time since last update) expires, whichever comes first.

Between updates, contracts read the last posted value, so an on-chain price can lag the market by up to the feed's deviation threshold or heartbeat, by design.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #51: Lending apps don't read prices from one exchange. Oracle networks like Chainlink combine prices from many sources and post them on-chain, but only when the price moves enough or after a set time.

Posting every second would cost too much gas. So between updates, apps use the last price posted, which may lag the market by up to the feed's update interval or price threshold.

card.title: Why on-chain prices can be stale
card.sub: Chainlink posts only after a large enough move, or when the heartbeat expires.

long: Sandwich attack (Zhou et al.): a pending DEX swap is visible before confirmation. A bot front-runs it to move y / x, lets the victim fill at a worse price, then back-runs to capture the move. The victim's slippage tolerance (amountOutMin) caps the loss, so it is the most a sandwich can take. Commit-reveal or fair-ordering schemes can prevent it.

#DeFi Mechanics #52: Sandwich attack (Zhou et al.): a pending DEX swap is visible before confirmation. A bot front-runs it to move y / x, lets the victim fill at a worse price, then back-runs to capture the move.

The victim's slippage tolerance (amountOutMin) caps the loss. Commit-reveal or fair-ordering schemes can prevent it.
simple:
#DeFi Mechanics #52: Your DEX swap is public before it's confirmed. A bot can buy just before you, let your trade push the price, then sell right after: a "sandwich". Your slippage setting is the most it can take.

Set slippage to 5% and a bot may take close to 5%. Keeping it tight, or using private transaction routes, limits what bots can grab.

card.title: The bot that wraps around your swap
card.sub: A bot buys just before you and sells right after. Your slippage setting caps the loss.

source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.14021 (Zhou et al., sandwich : front-run + back-run d'une tx vue sur le réseau P2P, limité par la slippage protection de la victime ; défenses commit-reveal / fair ordering)
